name: AOD-9604

lead: AOD-9604 is a synthetic peptide derived from the fat-metabolising region of human growth hormone, a modified version of its C-terminal fragment. It was developed in Australia as an obesity treatment and later sold as a research peptide for fat loss.

Human trials in obesity did not show clinically meaningful weight loss, and the developer discontinued the obesity program. It continues to be promoted in peptide marketing, although efficacy evidence in humans is limited.

paras: The peptide is proposed to mimic the lipolytic action of growth hormone without its effects on growth or blood sugar, stimulating fat breakdown and inhibiting fat formation in adipose tissue. Evidence for this comes from cell and animal studies, and the effect was not robustly observed in humans.

Short-term safety in clinical studies was described as similar to placebo, but long-term data are lacking. It is not approved as a drug in most countries, is sold as a research chemical of variable quality, and is prohibited in competitive sport by WADA. Human trials have not shown a clinically meaningful fat-loss benefit.

lead: AOD-9604 is a 16-amino-acid synthetic peptide based on residues 176 to 191 of human growth hormone (hGH), with a tyrosine substituted for the N-terminal phenylalanine. It was developed as a potential obesity treatment on the idea that this fragment retains growth hormone's fat-metabolizing action without its other effects [1][2].

Metabolic Pty developed it in Australia, with phase IIa trials underway by 2002 [3]. Wikipedia reports that early human trials suggested lipolytic activity without IGF-1 stimulation, that a 12-week randomized trial found participants lost on average 1.8 kg more than placebo, and that a later 24-week trial showed poor efficacy and development ended in 2007 [1].

It is not an approved drug in the sources reviewed. It is sold by research-peptide vendors for fat loss and is listed as prohibited by anti-doping rules [1][4]. Sources reviewed include only a single brief forum mention of its use [5].
infobox: Obesity program terminated in 2007 per Wikipedia

paras: AOD-9604 was developed for obesity treatment and is now marketed as a research peptide for fat loss [1][3]. Wikipedia describes it as orally active [1]. No approved indication exists in the sources reviewed.

Early studies characterized the metabolic effects of the synthetic lipolytic domain and its safety and tolerability in humans [2][6]. In a 12-week randomized trial participants receiving AOD-9604 lost on average 1.8 kg more than those on placebo, but development stopped after a 24-week trial showed poor efficacy [1]. Reviews from 2006 list it among obesity drugs in development as a human growth hormone fragment that increases adipose lipolysis [7].

A paper on its safety and tolerability in humans describes the peptide's short-term tolerability [6]. Long-term data are lacking in the sources reviewed. Supplies sold as research chemicals are not regulated, and reviews of peptide therapies describe a gray market of unapproved compounds outside regulatory oversight [8].

In mice AOD-9604 appears to enhance lipolysis by upregulating beta-3 adrenergic receptors; mice lacking that receptor do not show the effect [1]. Chronic treatment of obese mice with the fragment increased fat oxidation and reduced weight in an early study [9]. These are animal findings, and the human effect did not reach sufficient magnitude in the later trial [1].

AOD-9604 is banned in athletes and tested for in competition [1]. Anti-doping literature covers detection of non-approved peptides including this one, and a 2013 study found it does not interfere with the WADA hGH isoform immunoassay [4][10]. Reviews of peptide use in orthopedics and sports list it among peptides marketed to patients [11][8].
The sources reviewed contain little community material; a T Nation post lists AOD-9604 among peptides used while losing weight on another drug [5].

Phase IIa trials began around 2002, a 12-week randomized trial reported a 1.8 kg difference from placebo, and a 24-week trial reported poor efficacy, ending development in 2007 [3][1]. A tolerability study in humans has been published [6]. No published trial has tested AOD-9604 for facial appearance.

lore.intro: Community material on AOD-9604 is sparse; it appears as one item in peptide lists alongside other fat-loss compounds [5].

claims.claim: AOD-9604 burns fat like growth hormone without growth hormone's side effects.
It can be stacked with other peptides such as tesamorelin and IGF-1 LR3 for fat loss.

timeline.event: Metabolic and animal studies of the AOD9604 fragment published [2][9].
Development halted after a 24-week trial with poor efficacy [1].
